summary: This informational document creates IANA registries for Delay-Tolerant Networking protocols such as the Bundle Protocol. The research group had used ad hoc registries; since the specifications are stable and have multiple interoperable implementations, official ones are now set up.

plainLanguage.summary: Messages that travel through slow, disconnected networks use agreed numbers. This moves those lists from the researchers' notebook to the official keeper.

subtitle: How the Delay-Tolerant Networking research group handed its Bundle Protocol number lists to IANA.

tldr.problem: The DTN research group kept its Bundle Protocol code values in ad hoc registries on a wiki, but the specifications were stable and widely implemented, so the lists needed an official keeper.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes the IANA registries created for the Bundle Protocol: block types, version, two control-flag fields, status report flags and two sets of reason codes. It also reserves a few values that no earlier document or ad hoc registry had defined.
tldr.outcome: IANA now holds these registries, so new values are assigned under stated policies (such as Specification Required or RFC Required) instead of on a research group wiki.

facts.label: Registries created
facts.value: Seven, all for the Bundle Protocol

today: RFC 6255 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the hand-off of the Bundle Protocol registries to IANA, and the registries it describes are specified in terms of RFC 5050.

sections.title: Why the Registries Moved
sections.content:
The Delay-Tolerant Networking Research Group (DTNRG) defined protocols for the DTN architecture, including the Bundle Protocol (RFC 5050) and the Licklider Transmission Protocol (RFC 5326). Their specifications contain fields whose values must be tracked in a registry.

For its research work the group had created ad hoc registries. Because the specifications are stable and have multiple interoperable implementations, the group wanted to hand the registries to IANA for official custody. This document describes the actions IANA took.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers kept their own list of code numbers. Since the rules were settled, they asked the official list-keeper to take over.

sections.title: Flag Fields Encoded as SDNVs
sections.content:
Several Bundle Protocol fields are extensible bit flag fields encoded as Self-Delimiting Numeric Values (SDNVs), as defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 5050. For these fields the registry lists the meaning of each bit position in the unencoded value; the SDNV encoding then treats all those bits as one number when sending and receiving.

Because implementations are not required to handle SDNVs with more than 64 bits in their unencoded value, flag fields should be limited to 64 bit positions. Processing of SDNV-encoded flags is discussed in RFC 6256.
sections.plainLanguage: A row of on/off switches is read as one number. The list says what each switch means, and there are at most 64 switches.

sections.title: Value Registries
sections.content:
Five registries hold single values. The Bundle Block Type registry is an unsigned 8-bit value: 0 is reserved, 1 is the Bundle Payload Block, 2-191 are unassigned (Specification Required) and 192-255 are for private or experimental use, with no assignment by IANA. The Primary Bundle Protocol Version registry (policy RFC Required) reserves 0-5, assigns 6 to RFC 5050 and leaves 7-255 unassigned.

The Bundle Status Report Flags registry (RFC Required) uses 8 bits: the five assigned flags mean received, custody accepted, forwarded, delivered and deleted. The Bundle Status Report Reason Codes registry runs from 0 (no additional information) to 8 (block unintelligible), with 9-254 unassigned and 255 reserved. The Bundle Custody Signal Reason Codes registry is a 7-bit value: 0 means no additional information, 1-2 and 9-126 are unassigned, and 127 is reserved.

Values 0 (block type), 0-5 (version), 00000000 (status report flags), 255 and 127 (reason codes) were not defined in any document or in the ad hoc registry. The DTNRG agreed to reserve them in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each list is like a menu of numbered choices. Some numbers are taken, some are free, and a few are kept aside so nobody uses them by accident.

sections.title: Control Flag Registries
sections.content:
Two registries list bit positions (counted right to left), each with a maximum of 64 flag bit positions and a Specification Required policy. The Bundle Processing Control Flags include: bit 0 bundle is a fragment, bit 1 the data unit is an administrative record, bit 2 must not be fragmented, bit 3 custody transfer requested, bit 4 destination is a singleton, bit 5 application acknowledgement requested, bits 7-8 class of service priority, and bits 14-18 requests for reports on reception, custody acceptance, forwarding, delivery and deletion. Bits 21-63 are unassigned.

The Block Processing Control Flags cover bits 0-6: replicate the block in every fragment, send a status report if the block cannot be processed, delete the bundle if it cannot be processed, last block, discard the block if it cannot be processed, block was forwarded without being processed, and block contains an EID-reference field. Bits 7-63 are unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch in the row has a job, such as 'do not break this package into pieces' or 'tell me when it arrives'. The list says which switch does what.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content: The document only requests registries managed by IANA, so it says there are no security issues involved and refers readers to the Security Considerations of the referenced protocols. In the IANA Considerations section, IANA states that it has created the registries described in the earlier sections.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing down a list of numbers does not open any new doors for trouble. The real safety rules live in the protocols themselves.
